episode_title: The Greatest Productivity Mantra: Kaator Re Bhaaji!

stories.summary: Jose Custodio de Faria, born in 1756 in Candolim, Goa, was a child prodigy invited to Lisbon to deliver a sermon before the Queen of Portugal. On stage in front of all the royalty, the boy froze. His father leaned forward and whispered in Konkani: 'Kaator re bhaaji, kaator re bhaaji' — these are all just vegetables; cut the vegetables, cut the vegetables. The boy recovered, went on to take part in the French Revolution, became one of the fathers of hypnotism, and was immortalised as a character in Dumas' The Count of Monte Cristo.
stories.insight: The greatest antidote to performance anxiety is task-reduction: don't worry about the audience or stakes, just do the next concrete unit of work. Most projects in life ultimately come down to chopping vegetables, again and again — the prestige is incidental, the chopping is the thing.

stories.summary: A teacher split a class in two. Group A had a week to research and produce one perfect pot — they read books, took online courses, theorised about technique. Group B was simply asked to produce as many pots as possible. At the end of the week, the best pots came from Group B. They had iterated, broken pots, learned from each one — while Group A was still optimising in their heads.
stories.insight: You get something right by getting it done — again and again and again. The block of stone has to exist before Rodin can carve The Thinker out of it; the first draft is the block of stone. Iteration beats theorisation in almost every creative discipline.

stories.topic: Ali Abdaal Took 26 Weeks to 1,000 Subscribers
stories.summary: When Ali Abdaal hit a million subscribers, he showed the curve of his growth. After 26 weeks of two videos per week — fifty videos in — he had only 1,000 subscribers. His advice: make two videos a week for two years before even looking at metrics. Anyone driven by validation in the early phase will quit before they get good.
stories.insight: Creators overestimate the short term and underestimate the long term. If you optimise for early validation, you will quit before you become good enough to deserve any. The only way through the doldrums is to do the work because you love it, not because anyone is watching.

stories.topic: How EIE Itself Was Procrastinated For A Year
stories.summary: Amit and Ajay had been talking about doing this show since August 2022 — they were debating names in Udaipur over a year before Episode 1. Ajay frames the gap as wisdom: dreams of quality kept them from launching too messy. Amit pushes back hard: 'I was procrastinating, not getting the job done, not doing any prep.' What finally broke the logjam was a chance brainstorm with their producer Vartika.
stories.insight: Beware of dressing up procrastination as preparation. Sharpening the axe is real (Lincoln) but most of the time we're just delaying. The truer rule for most creators: when in doubt, jump.

stories.topic: India Uncut and 8,000 Posts Without Anxiety
stories.summary: Amit started his blog India Uncut around 2003-04 with five posts a day. Over five active years he wrote about eight thousand posts. There was no anxiety about getting any single post perfect — it was him thinking aloud. Much of it would embarrass him today, but it was the journey that made him a better writer and thinker.
stories.insight: Volume in public is a forge. Embarrassing-looking output is not a failure of the work — it is the work. You can only become a better writer by being a worse one in public, repeatedly.

stories.topic: The Sportsman Who Ran In The Rain
stories.summary: In an interview Amit read in the early 2000s — sounds like Dravid but isn't him — a top sportsperson was asked: what is your greatest talent? The reply: 'If I run every day at five, but one morning I wake up with a cold, I've achieved my goals for the year, my holiday is coming up, it's raining outside, and I just don't feel like going — I will still get up and go running in the rain. That's talent.'
stories.insight: Talent is not the natural skill we glamourise — it is the psychological quality of showing up unconditionally. Discipline, dressed up. The greatest performers are not those with the best gifts but those who can override the body and weather and mood when none of them are cooperating.

stories.topic: The Indian Sorting Machine and Mathematics
stories.summary: Ajay was 'that lucky child' who happened to blossom early in mathematics — and suddenly everyone painted a number on his forehead. He has watched the same machinery be cruel to others. India sorts kids early as smart or dumb, often around mathematics, and treats the label as destiny. He and Nitin Pai are planning to write 'heretical things' about the IIT JEE exam.
stories.insight: Educationists know what India's testing apparatus refuses to admit: different humans blossom at different ages and on different dimensions. Putting an eight-year-old number on a forehead and treating it as destiny is an industrial-revolution-era convenience masquerading as merit.

stories.topic: The Habit of Organising Life Around Reading
stories.summary: When asked what habit he is glad he built, Ajay's answer is single-pointed: he has organised everything else in his life around the project of getting more hours per day to read. He pushes away mundane decisions, reduces the burden of everyday life, and protects time for the page.
stories.insight: A purposeful life is largely a subtraction problem. Getting better at one thing is mostly about ruthlessly removing all the other things. Most lives drift; a few are designed around a singular question.

stories.topic: Rahul Dravid On Not Comparing Himself To Tendulkar
stories.summary: Ajay once attended a talk by Rahul Dravid where Dravid said: 'I did not think about Sachin Tendulkar. I only tried to be the best Rahul Dravid that I can be.' Ajay holds this up as an antidote to credentialism and Louis-Vuitton-bag thinking — instead of optimising for external markers, you orient your operating system around your own irreducible journey.
stories.insight: Comparison is the death of purpose. Even the second-best batsman of his generation found his durability by refusing to compete with the first-best. The real engine is internal: be the best version of yourself, not a worse version of someone else.

stories.topic: Donald Knuth, TeX, and a Bug-Free Taj Mahal
stories.summary: Donald Knuth spent decades polishing TeX, the typesetting system used to publish many of the world's great books. In old age he declared it finished — every feature he wanted is there, no recorded bugs, and the source is open for anyone to extend (just call your fork something else). When a rare bug is found, Knuth himself writes a personal cheque to the finder, who frames it on the wall. He calls TeX his Taj Mahal.
stories.insight: Software culture worships novelty and disruption — Knuth represents the lost virtue of finishing things. A bug-free, mature, complete tool is a kind of art most of the industry has forgotten how to make. Sometimes the highest craftsmanship is to lay down the chisel.

recommendations.creator: James Clear
recommendations.context: James Clear's book on the science of habit formation.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it the best book on productivity he has read and a rabbit hole into many others. Its central line — 'habits are the compound interest of self-improvement' — captures why habits, not goals, are the whole game. If you only read one productivity book, start here.

recommendations.creator: Ali Abdaal
recommendations.context: Productivity-focused YouTuber who started small and grew to over a million subscribers.
recommendations.reason: Abdaal is living his own advice — he ground through 50 videos and 26 weeks before hitting 1,000 subscribers — which gives his advice on tools, mental models and frameworks unusual credibility. His parable of patience for creators is the heart of this episode.

recommendations.creator: Thomas Frank
recommendations.context: Another productivity-focused YouTuber.
recommendations.reason: Pair with Ali Abdaal as Amit's two go-to channels for figuring out which productivity tools, mental models and frameworks fit your own working style.

recommendations.context: The original Unix operating system and its command-line interface, now under the hood of macOS, ChromeOS, Android, Kindle and Linux — everything but Windows.
recommendations.reason: Ajay's single biggest productivity recommendation. The Unix philosophy — small focused tools, easy to string together — is the most powerful and productive computing environment he has ever used in forty years around computers. The shell is not forbidding; it is freedom.

recommendations.creator: Richard Stallman
recommendations.context: Editor in active development since the 1960s, with a fully programmable Lisp interface and 5,000+ third-party extensions.
recommendations.reason: Not just an editor but a foundation: write a hundred lines of Lisp and you've built your own productivity world on top of one of the world's most mature pieces of software. The survivorship bias is the feature — an editor that has retained passionate users for sixty years has earned the trust.

recommendations.context: An Emacs mode that approximates much of Roam Research's networked-thought capability for a single user.
recommendations.reason: Plays the same role Roam plays for Amit — nested entries, cross-linking, structured thinking — only locally and freely. Lacks Roam's collaboration, but for a solo workflow Ajay considers it a fully credible Swiss Army knife.

recommendations.context: A free knowledge-base tool used by Pranay Kotasthane and others at Takshashila that stores notes as plain Markdown files.
recommendations.reason: Markdown storage means the entire Unix toolchain works on your notes — grep, sed, awk, whatever you like — so your second brain isn't trapped inside one company's app. A practical halfway house between Roam's polish and Emacs's depth.

recommendations.creator: Conor White-Sullivan
recommendations.context: Networked-thought note-taking app based on the German Zettelkasten system, with bi-directional links and infinite nesting.
recommendations.reason: Amit's daily driver and game-changer. Demonstrated live in the episode for prepping the Ghazala Wahab episode, the Ukraine episode, and the previous EIE on freedom — the form of the tool literally shaped how he thought through each. The brain is a messy, impressionistic machine; Roam is his second brain.

recommendations.creator: Tiago Forte
recommendations.context: Tiago Forte's course on using technology to augment the brain's poor knowledge-retention.
recommendations.reason: Names the central problem of modern reading: 'all day we are taking in learnings that we do not retain.' Forte's framework gives you a way to externalise and reuse what would otherwise wash through you.

recommendations.item: Praise for intelligence can undermine children's motivation and performance
recommendations.creator: Claudia Mueller and Carol Dweck
recommendations.context: Foundational psychology paper showing that praising effort beats praising intelligence in children.
recommendations.reason: Amit's evidence base for 'verbs over adjectives.' Kids praised as 'smart' get a sense of entitlement, stop trying as hard, sometimes cheat; kids praised for effort and persistence keep improving. A profound rule for parenting and self-talk.

recommendations.item: Huberman Lab episode on growth mindset
recommendations.creator: Andrew Huberman
recommendations.context: Episode of the Huberman Lab podcast unpacking the Mueller-Dweck research and growth mindset more broadly.
recommendations.reason: How Amit found his way into the Mueller-Dweck paper. Recommended as a clean entry point for anyone who wants to understand why effort-based feedback matters in their own and their kids' lives.

recommendations.item: Doing better than a competitive exam
recommendations.creator: Nitin Pai and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay and Nitin Pai's piece challenging the cultural deference to the IIT JEE.
recommendations.reason: The seed of the larger book they are planning on the harms of India's monolithic competitive-exam regime — the relentless sorting that paints numbers on children's foreheads and treats labels as destiny.

recommendations.creator: Ghazala Wahab
recommendations.context: Ghazala Wahab's book on being Muslim in India.
recommendations.reason: Used as the live demo for Amit's Roam workflow, showing how he extracts and links chapter-level notes. The 'shelling pine nuts' image of her grandfather is held up as a gold-standard example of show-don't-tell writing.

recommendations.item: Narendra Shenoy and Mr Narendra Shenoy (Episode 250, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Narendra Shenoy
recommendations.context: Amit's episode with his good friend Narendra Shenoy — the friend who made the 'Kaator Re Bhaaji' T-shirt that Amit and Ajay are wearing.
recommendations.reason: Origin of the t-shirt and a window into Shenoy's wit. Functions as the sociable backstory to the episode's central slogan.

recommendations.item: The Life and Times of Jerry Pinto (Episode 314, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Jerry Pinto
recommendations.context: Eight-and-a-half-hour oral-history conversation with the writer Jerry Pinto.
recommendations.reason: The episode where Amit first heard the Abbe Faria / Kaator Re Bhaaji story from Jerry Pinto. Recommended as a fantastic deep dive in its own right.

recommendations.creator: Alexandre Dumas
recommendations.context: Dumas' classic novel.
recommendations.reason: Features a character named after Abbe Faria — the same Goan boy from Candolim who was hissed at to cut the vegetables. A nice doorway from the productivity mantra into world literature.

recommendations.item: The BJP Before Modi (Episode 202, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Vinay Sitapati
recommendations.context: Amit's first long-form episode with Vinay Sitapati.
recommendations.reason: Source of the line Amit quotes from Sitapati: 'Never let perfection be the enemy of production.' A whole hour of writing-process discussion compressed into one practical aphorism.

recommendations.item: Being Muslim in India (Episode 216, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Ghazala Wahab
recommendations.context: Amit's episode with Ghazala Wahab on her book Born a Muslim.
recommendations.reason: The companion episode to the book Amit demos in his Roam workflow. The conversation that the chapter-by-chapter notes were built around.

recommendations.item: A Deep Dive Into Ukraine vs Russia (Episode 335, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit's deep dive with Ajay on the Russia-Ukraine war.
recommendations.reason: Used in the Roam demo to show that the episode wasn't a quick prep job but the harvest of a lifetime's reading — Ajay's chapter-by-chapter notes with sources, rabbit holes, links. A worked example of reading-as-life-organising-principle.

recommendations.item: Why Freedom Matters (Episode 10 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: The previous EIE episode on liberalisation and freedom.
recommendations.reason: Demoed in the Roam walkthrough to show how Amit and Ajay structure their joint preparation — Amit's spiel on Angus Maddison and pre-91 India, Ajay's Bhagwati and Friedman quotes, parts they used and parts they cut on the fly.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's 2008 piece on Indian education.
recommendations.reason: The piece where he developed his 'supermarket' metaphor: in shampoo and biscuits we have a thousand brands to pick from, but in education and other fields that really count, markets are not allowed to function and our children pay the cost.

recommendations.creator: Richard Dawkins
recommendations.context: Dawkins' book on atheism.
recommendations.reason: Pointed at as the source (or possibly Hitchens) of the line that everyone is already an atheist about thousands of religions — they just stop one short. A useful frame for the larger humility argument that we are all stupid about most things.

recommendations.context: All-in-one productivity and document tool.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it a great productivity tool that he has not yet adopted, mentioned for readers who want a more structured workspace than Roam's loosely-organised knowledge graph.

recommendations.context: Industry-standard screenplay-writing software.
recommendations.reason: Mentioned as the dedicated tool for screenplay form when Amit fantasises about a one-tool-does-everything workflow.

recommendations.context: Long-form writing software popular with novelists.
recommendations.reason: Paired with Final Draft as one of the dedicated form-specific writing tools Amit has tried and admired.

recommendations.creator: David Allen
recommendations.context: David Allen's classic on personal task management — the source of GTD ('do, defer, delegate').
recommendations.reason: Mentioned as the seminal text for the productivity-tools-and-techniques tradition, even as Amit and Ajay riff on its limits.

recommendations.creator: Walt Whitman
recommendations.context: Whitman's poem with the famous line about contradicting oneself.
recommendations.reason: Source of Amit's permission to contradict himself within a single episode: 'Do I contradict myself? Very well, then I contradict myself; I am large, I contain multitudes.' The whole argument structure of the episode (just do it / just be it / just do it) leans on it.

core_ideas.explanation: The episode's spinal mantra. Whatever your task — sermon before a queen, paper, song, video, novel — its prestige melts away when you reduce it to its concrete unit of work. The vegetables in front of you are vegetables. The work is to chop. This is also an antidote to performance anxiety: you cannot freeze if you have stopped thinking of the audience and started thinking of the next bullet point.
core_ideas.quote: All these are vegetables. Cut the vegetables, cut the vegetables, cut the vegetables.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit's first slogan. In any creative project there is a trade-off between getting it done and getting it right; you should bias hard toward done. The first draft is a brain-dump — Rodin had a block of stone before he had The Thinker. You get something right by getting it done, again and again. Vinay Sitapati's version: 'Never let perfection be the enemy of production.'
core_ideas.quote: How do you get it right? You get it right by getting it done again and again and again.

core_ideas.concept: Don't Do It, Just Be It (Identity-Based Habits)
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's second slogan, contradicting the first. Goal-driven habits ('I will read an hour every evening') collapse on the third day, dent your self-image, and send you spiralling. Identity-driven habits ('I am a self-taught polymath; when I am bored I pick up a book, not the phone') flow naturally from who you have decided you are. Self-image drives habits; habits do not, by themselves, sustain self-image. Best version of you first, behaviours after.
core_ideas.quote: The good habits flow from there. Then you don't need to set a time.

core_ideas.concept: Don't Be It, Just Do It (Verbs Over Adjectives)
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's third slogan, contradicting the second. Adjectives label ('you are smart,' 'you are talented') and create entitlement and fragility — Mueller and Dweck found that kids praised as intelligent stop putting in effort and sometimes cheat. Verbs describe action ('you tried hard,' 'you persisted') and grow. Amit's regret: too much of his life he traded on a label that came easy, when the people who had to work twenty hours for what he did in twenty minutes were learning a more useful skill.

Amit's fourth and master frame. Take a hundred writers — ask their goals, you can't sort them; ask their processes and habits, you can predict who will make it, almost always correctly. Habits are the compound interest of self-improvement. Set absurdly small daily targets — write 200 words a day, not 1000 — because a missed target dents the identity. Build the muscle. An annual gym membership is not enough; reading bodybuilding books is not enough; you have to actually go.
core_ideas.quote: Habits are the compound interest of self-improvement.

core_ideas.concept: Ajay's Tempering: Quality Standards Matter Too
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's pushback on pure 'just do it.' India venerates 'jugaad' — a fancy name for people who do things badly and never reach for excellence. Iterative refinement only works if you are climbing a hill — there must be a sense of gradient, of standards, of 'no, this ain't good enough, can we try harder?' Without that quality compass, repetition produces a thousand mediocre pots, not a great one. Bias for action and bias for quality must coexist.
core_ideas.quote: There are miracles of quality that can be achieved.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's concrete protocol. Habit formation takes about two to three months of focused, conscious attention on a single area. After that, the habit is on autopilot and demands little cognitive load — but you must keep watching it from the corner of your eye to make sure it has not silently wilted. You can only fight one habit at a time; the queue is serial, not parallel. Then you can move to the next.
core_ideas.quote: You can't do six things at a time. You have to fight one thing at a time.

core_ideas.concept: The Anxiety Of What Others Think (And Its Dissolution)
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's diagnosis of the deepest human anxiety — what others will think — and his middle-aged answer: 'no one is thinking of you, boss. Everyone's got their heads up their own ass.' Once you accept that no one is taking notes on you, you can stop projecting a self for social media's comparison economy and start tending an actual self.
core_ideas.quote: I find it profoundly problematic that we live too much of our lives on social media, where we compare our real selves with the projected selves of others.

core_ideas.explanation: An extension of the Hitchens/Dawkins line — every theist is already an atheist about thousands of religions, just one short. Similarly, every human is stupid about almost everything. We each know one or two domains tolerably well; in the vast remainder we are children. This produces both humility about ourselves and a refusal to denigrate others for not being good at the narrow things we happen to value.
core_ideas.quote: I will postulate that we are all stupid.

core_ideas.concept: Curiosity And Endurance As The Two Superpowers
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's deepest philosophical frame. Forget 'talent' — the word is harmful. The superpowers that actually carry a long life are curiosity (to keep learning) and endurance (to keep going). They sit on top of purpose. Without purpose, you orient around 'Louis Vuitton bags' — a journal pub, a degree, a job, a Paris trip — and once you have them you crash, because they were never the point. With purpose, the year-long clock of life is no longer the same year repeated thirty times.
core_ideas.quote: The two superpowers are curiosity and endurance.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's metaphor for a poor operating system: organising your life around tangible-marker rewards — degrees, journal pubs, festival invitations, even cities visited. These are weak engines because they don't harness the mind, and once obtained they leave a vacuum. Worst inside academia, where 'journal orientation' switches off curiosity by channelling it through external referees. Conservatives and order-lovers face a related problem: same year repeated, no challenge, no growth.
core_ideas.quote: What is the meaning of life? Once you finished with getting those three papers.

core_ideas.concept: The Form Of Your Tool Shapes The Form Of Your Thought
core_ideas.explanation: Amit on why his note-taking matters. Reading a physical book all day produces one rhythm of mind; doomscrolling produces a choppier one with shorter attention spans. The structure of Roam Research — nested entries, bidirectional links — pushed Amit to think in a more structured way than Microsoft Word and Ctrl-F ever did. Tool form is not neutral. Pick your form, because it will pick your thinking.
core_ideas.quote: The form of our input and output matters.

core_ideas.explanation: Tiago Forte's frame, taken seriously by Amit. The brain is a flawed, impressionistic, leaky knowledge-machine — every day we take in more learnings than we retain. The answer is to externalise: a digital companion organ that holds notes, links, quotes and structures, so that the wet-brain can think while the second brain remembers. Roam, Obsidian, Org Mode are all instantiations of the same idea.

core_ideas.concept: Old, Mature, Boring Things Can Be The Best
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's contrarian software claim. The world idolises the recent and the current; he suggests that great old things — Unix, Emacs, TeX — outperform almost everything new. The trick is survivorship bias as a feature: an editor that has retained passionate users for sixty years is signalling something the latest VC-funded launch cannot. Knuth's TeX is the limit case — finished software, no recorded bugs, completed in old age and handed to the future.

Small focused tools that each do one thing well, easy to string together to perform any task. Ajay holds it up as the most fertile pathway to harnessing computers. Not just an operating system but a way of thinking — the same set of ideas seeded TCP/IP, the internet, and the World Wide Web. When asked who the greatest man of the last fifty years is, Ajay's answer was Ken Thompson.

core_ideas.concept: The Greatest Man of the Last 50 Years
core_ideas.explanation: An off-hand claim worth its own line: Ajay names Ken Thompson — co-creator of Unix and many of the foundational ideas of modern computing — as the most important figure of the last half-century. The implicit argument: the substrate beneath the substrate of modern life was built largely by him.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit on the slogans war: 'We are at the brink of a great moment in merchandising where the slogan Just Do It is going to be overpowered by the slogan Kaator Re Bhaaji.'
Amit clarifying Abbe Faria's parents: his father was a priest and mother was a nun, but 'don't worry, no hanky panky' — they joined the church after having him.
Amit's social-media reality check: 'No one is taking screenshots and waiting to put it on Twitter to shame you. Or actually in my case they are. But you know, so it's cool.'

Amit on his own privilege at being smart-by-default: people who had to study for twenty hours could be matched by him in twenty minutes — a great trap, because you never learn how to actually work hard.
Ajay riffing on academic envy: 'It is not only academics who want pubs. I was once in Europe, it was a hot sunny day in Vienna, maybe Bratislava.' (English-speakers' double meaning of 'pub.')

Amit's bilingual gag on Knuth's bug-free TeX: 'What does a Marathi programmer say to another Marathi programmer when he finds a flaw? Bug, bug.' ('Bug' in Marathi is roughly equivalent to a vulgar reference to female anatomy.)
Amit ribbing Ajay for skipping his recommendation in the previous episode: 'You weren't prepared, which is a great flaw in your productivity processes — after all these things that you say.'
Ajay on the Indian sorting machine: he was 'that lucky child' who happened to blossom early, and 'suddenly everybody was painting a number on my forehead.'
'Kaator re bhaaji' (Konkani: cut the vegetables) — the Faria family's whispered antidote to performance anxiety, hissed by Senior Faria at his frozen prodigy son in front of the Queen of Portugal.

Walt Whitman's 'Song of Myself, 51': 'Do I contradict myself? Very well, then I contradict myself; I am large, I contain multitudes.' Cited by Amit to justify offering four mutually-contradictory productivity slogans in one episode.

Abraham Lincoln on preparation: 'If you give me six hours to chop a tree, I'll spend five hours sharpening the axe.' Used by Ajay; pushed back on by Amit, who said in their case the year of waiting was just procrastination, not axe-sharpening.
Christopher Hitchens / Richard Dawkins (Amit isn't sure which): every theist is already an atheist about thousands of other religions — they just stop one short of the full set.
Auguste Rodin and The Thinker — the sculptor did not summon the figure from thin air; he started with a block of stone and edited. Amit's metaphor for the first draft.
Rahul Dravid on Sachin Tendulkar: 'I did not think about Sachin Tendulkar. I only tried to be the best Rahul Dravid that I can be.' Ajay's gold-standard articulation of purpose without comparison.

Ali Abdaal's Parable of the Pottery Class — the now-famous version of the quality-vs-quantity experiment, where the group graded on volume produced the best pots. (Originally from Bayles and Orland's Art and Fear, popularised by Abdaal's video.)
Donald Knuth's TeX bounty — when a rare bug is found in TeX, Knuth himself writes a personal cheque to the finder, who then frames it on the wall instead of cashing it.
Zettelkasten — the 20th-century German index-card knowledge system (most famously Niklas Luhmann's) that Roam Research is descended from.
GTD ('do, defer, delegate') — David Allen's Getting Things Done, the canonical productivity framework Ajay has to coax out of Amit's memory mid-episode.
Vinay Sitapati's writing maxim: 'Never let perfection be the enemy of production.' Quoted by Amit from his first long episode with Sitapati.
